decisions.quote:
Berinsky et al. (2012) demonstrated the validity of
MTurk by replicating classic experiments originally conducted on probability samples; we follow their lead and do

the same on Lucid. As an empirical matter, our Lucid replications recover very similar treatment effect estimates to the
original studies.
decisions.reason: Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz (2012) is not a tested original finding; it supplies the methodological validation template (evaluating an online convenience platform by comparing respondent characteristics to national benchmarks and replicating classic survey experiments) and serves as an earlier MTurk replication benchmark. While the abstract refers to Berinsky et al. (2012) as the 'point of departure' whose analyses are replicated on Lucid, the full text explicitly clarifies that Berinsky et al. (2012) demonstrated MTurk's validity by replicating classic experiments and that the authors 'follow their lead and do the same on Lucid' by replicating five specific original survey experiments (2014 GSS welfare wording, Tversky and Kahneman 1981, Kam and Simas 2010, Hiscox 2006, and Berinsky 2017; Table 1 and Experiments 1-5, pp. 4, 6-9), scaling estimates against the original experiments. Under the codebook, a work that supplies the validation method or an earlier replication attempt not itself re-tested is not a target, and because the paper tests five distinct original studies rather than a single replacement target, this method/template row is removed.

decisions.quote:
In the Welfare,
Asian Disease, Kam and Simas, Hiscox and Berinsky facets found in Figure 2, we present standardized treatment
effect estimates, where we have scaled the outcome variables for Lucid and MTurk by the mean and standard deviation of the original experiments. The Berinsky facet does
not include an MTurk estimate since it has not been previously replicated on an MTurk sample.
decisions.reason: Outcomes are original-specific and depend on resolving a valid tested original identity. Because the shipped original (Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz 2012) is a removed methodological template/benchmark row rather than a tested original study, no replication outcome applies to it. Furthermore, the shipped 'mixed' outcome and quote from the abstract conflate descriptive demographic benchmarking (against the 2012 ANES), four replicated experiments that succeeded (2014 GSS welfare wording, Tversky and Kahneman 1981, Kam and Simas 2010, and Hiscox 2006), and a fifth experiment on ACA 'death panel' rumors (Berinsky 2017) that was never part of Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz (2012) at all.

decisions.quote:
In our empirical section, we replicate five survey experiments that were originally conducted on other samples. As
an exercise, we read each paper with an eye towards understanding whether the theory under study should, in principle,
apply to the sorts of people who participate in online surveys.
decisions.location: when are convenience samples fit for purpose?, p. 3 (lines 245-247)
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind codings agree that the paper is a replication study collecting new survey experimental data (N = 3,504 on Lucid) to re-test previously published experimental findings.

decisions.location: Experiments, Experiment 1: Welfare spending, p. 6 (lines 455-466); Treatment effect heterogeneity, p. 9 (lines 571-587); References, pp. 13-14
decisions.quote:
Experiment 1: Welfare spending
Our first experiment replicates a classic question wording
experiment. Control subjects are asked whether we are
spending too little, about right, or too much on “welfare.”
Treatment subjects are asked the same question about
“Assistance to the poor” or “Caring for the poor.” The
General Social Survey (GSS) has conducted this experiment
every other year since 1984; we use the 2014 GSS estimate
as the baseline result. This experiment behaves on Lucid
much as it does on MTurk and the GSS – a large increase in
support for redistribution when the question is phrased as
assistance or caring for the poor rather than as “welfare.”
decisions.reason: In Experiment 1 (Welfare spending), the authors empirically conduct the classic welfare versus assistance/caring for the poor question-wording experiment on Lucid (N = 3,504) and compare the treatment effect estimates against the 2014 General Social Survey (GSS) baseline result (and 2016 GSS conditional average treatment effects by race/ethnicity). However, the primary source text and reference list do not cite or identify any specific published original paper or bibliographic dataset entry for the recurring GSS welfare spending experiment (nor for what p. 9 refers to as 'the original iteration of this experiment'), leaving authors, year, title, and DOI blank in the blind candidate. The sole welfare-related citation in the section, Gilens (1996), is explicitly described as subsequent work identifying race as a moderator ('Though this is not one of the factors theorized to condition the phrasing treatment effect in the original iteration of this experiment, race has since been identified as perhaps the single most important influencing factor in position on welfare spending (Gilens, 1996)'). Shipped row 462 (Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz 2012, 10.1093/pan/mpr057) is the methodological validation template removed in prior adjudication (prior state file absent). The precise unresolved question is what specific source-backed original bibliographic identity (authors, year, title) corresponds to the GSS welfare spending experiment in Experiment 1.

corrected_value.title: The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice.

decisions.location: Experiments, Experiment 2: Asian Disease problem, pp. 6-7 (lines 468-500); Table 1, p. 4 (lines 287-288); References, p. 14 (lines 1005-1006)
decisions.quote:
Experiment 2: Asian Disease problem
Our second experiment is also a classic, this time of the
behavioral economics literature. Tversky and Kahneman
(1981) show that people take the riskier option when in a
“loss frame” rather than a “gain frame.” Subjects are asked
to “Imagine that your country is preparing for the outbreak
of an unusual disease, which is expected to kill 600 people.
Two alternative programs to combat the disease have been
proposed.” Subjects in the control condition are told: “If
Program A is adopted, 200 people will be saved. If Program
B is adopted, there is one-third probability that 600 people
will be saved, and two-third probability that no people will
be saved.” Subjects in the treatment group (the “mortality
frame”) are told: “If Program A is adopted, 400 people will
die. If Program B is adopted there is one-third probability
that nobody will die, and two-third probability that 600 people will die.”
decisions.reason: In Experiment 2, the authors empirically re-test Tversky and Kahneman's (1981) Asian Disease framing experiment on a new Lucid sample, scaling treatment effect estimates by the mean and standard deviation of the original experiment and comparing the gain-versus-loss framing effect across the original undergraduate sample, MTurk, and Lucid (Figure 2). The original work is explicitly identified in the text, Table 1, and the reference list as Tversky A and Kahneman D (1981) 'The framing of decisions and the psychology of choice', Science 211(4481): 453-458 (no DOI printed). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 462: Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz 2012, 10.1093/pan/mpr057, removed in prior adjudication; prior state file absent) is a 2012 Political Analysis methodological paper on MTurk that supplies the validation template, not an alternate report of Tversky and Kahneman (1981), and none of the sibling targets (0, 2, 3, 4) duplicate this 1981 original.

decisions.location: Experiments, Experiment 3: Framing and risk, pp. 7-8 (lines 502-519); Treatment effect heterogeneity, p. 9 (lines 588-592); References, p. 14 (lines 956-957)
decisions.quote:
This finding was replicated in
both MTurk and Lucid samples. Receiving the mortality
frame increases the likelihood of selecting the probabilistic
choice. Risk acceptance correlates with choosing the risky
option, but does not moderate the effect of treatment, as we
will discuss in greater depth.
decisions.reason: In Experiment 3, the authors explicitly re-test Kam and Simas (2010) on a new Lucid sample, examining both the main effect of the mortality frame and whether baseline risk acceptance correlates with risky choice without moderating the mortality-frame treatment effect, and comparing standardized estimates and heterogeneity against the original study (Figures 2 and 3). The original study is identified in Table 1, the Experiment 3 heading/text, Note 11, and the reference list as Kam CD and Simas EN (2010) 'Risk orientations and policy frames', The Journal of Politics 72(2): 381-396 (no DOI printed). It is distinct from Target 1 (Tversky and Kahneman 1981, which did not test the risk-acceptance moderation hypothesis examined by Kam and Simas 2010, as Note 11 explains) and from shipped row 462 (Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz 2012, 10.1093/pan/mpr057, the methodological validation template removed in prior adjudication; prior state file absent), so report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.title: Through a glass and darkly: Attitudes toward international trade and the curious effects of issue framing.

decisions.location: Experiments, Experiment 4: Free trade, pp. 8-9 (lines 521-537); Treatment effect heterogeneity, p. 9 (lines 593-605); References, p. 14 (lines 950-952)
decisions.quote:
Study 4 is a replication of Hiscox (2006), which measured the
effects of positive, negative, and expert opinion frames on
support for free trade. The study employed a 2 × 4 design.
decisions.reason: In Experiment 4 (Study 4), the authors empirically replicate the 2 x 4 free-trade issue-framing and expert-opinion experiment of Hiscox (2006) on a new Lucid sample, comparing main treatment effects (Figure 2) and treatment effect heterogeneity by college education and expert-opinion condition (Figure 4) against the original sample. The original paper is explicitly identified in Table 1, Experiment 4, and the reference list as Hiscox MJ (2006) 'Through a glass and darkly: Attitudes toward international trade and the curious effects of issue framing', International Organization 60(03): 755-780 (no DOI printed). The sole shipped row (input_row_index 462: Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz 2012, 10.1093/pan/mpr057, removed in prior adjudication; prior state file absent) is a different study by different authors on MTurk validation, and no sibling target duplicates Hiscox (2006).

corrected_value.title: Rumors and health care reform: Experiments in political misinformation.

decisions.location: Experiments, Experiment 5: Healthcare rumors, p. 9 (lines 539-561); Treatment effect heterogeneity, p. 9 (lines 606-619); Discussion, p. 12 (lines 736-750); References, p. 13 (lines 875-877)
decisions.quote:
We conclude our set of five experiments with a note of caution. We attempted to replicate Berinsky’s 2017 experiment
on belief in rumors surrounding the Affordable Care Act
(ACA), specifically the false rumor that the ACA would
create “death panels” that would make end-of-life decisions
for patients without their consent. In the original experiment (conducted in 2010 on a sample provided by Survey
Sampling International (SSI)), a large portion of the sample
believed the rumor, and corrections delivered by
Republicans, Democrats, and Nonpartisan groups were all
effective in correcting false beliefs.
decisions.reason: In Experiment 5, the authors empirically re-test Berinsky's (2017) experiment on correcting ACA 'death panel' misinformation using a new Lucid sample, comparing baseline rumor belief, average treatment effects (Figure 2), and partisan conditional average treatment effects (Figure 5) directly against the original 2010 SSI sample reported in Berinsky (2017). The reference list identifies this target as Berinsky AJ (2017) 'Rumors and health care reform: Experiments in political misinformation', British Journal of Political Science 47(2): 241-262 (no DOI printed). Although Adam J. Berinsky is also first author of shipped row 462 (Berinsky, Huber, and Lenz 2012, 10.1093/pan/mpr057, 'Evaluating Online Labor Markets for Experimental Research: Amazon.com's Mechanical Turk', Political Analysis 20(3): 351-368, removed in prior adjudication; prior state file absent), the two works are substantively distinct studies—indeed, p. 6 (line 447) explicitly notes that the Berinsky (2017) experiment 'has not been previously replicated on an MTurk sample'—so report equivalence does not apply.
